title: Reinforcement Learning for Shared Autonomy in Powered Wheelchair Navigation
abstract: This work addresses assistive robotics for powered wheelchairs using deep reinforcement learning. The researcher developed three key contributions: (1) a mapless autonomous navigation system trained in virtual environments and validated against established path planning methods, (2) a novel shared control framework using reinforcement learning that accepts noisy user input while maintaining safety—reducing collisions significantly in trials, and (3) a vision-based head-control interface using face detection as an alternative to joystick control. The research demonstrates that when the shared control system combines with the head-control interface, results show a remarkable 92% reduction in collisions while improving user autonomy and safety outcomes in real-world testing scenarios.
relevance_note: Directly develops a RL-based shared autonomy framework for powered wheelchairs with experimental collision-reduction results.

title: A decision-theoretic approach for the collaborative control of a smart wheelchair
abstract: The research presents a framework enabling shared control between human operators and robotic systems in wheelchair navigation. Using a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), the system combines user inputs with autonomous intelligence to optimize collaborative actions while accounting for uncertainty in user intent, commands, and environmental conditions. Key findings from testing on the SmartWheeler platform with eight participants demonstrate that this approach improves navigation efficiency and usability compared to manual control alone. Participants experienced significantly less cognitive workload using collaborative control, allowing them to focus on secondary tasks while maintaining safe navigation. The system operates through two main components: a prediction module estimating user goals from sensor and input data, and an assistance module selecting actions that minimize expected user costs while respecting their intent.
relevance_note: Core POMDP-based shared control framework validated on the SmartWheeler platform with user study demonstrating reduced cognitive workload.

title: The effect of robotic wheelchair control paradigm and interface on user performance, effort and preference: An experimental assessment
abstract: How control is distributed between a human operator and an autonomous system significantly impacts assistive robots designed to support individuals with severe motor impairments. Despite this importance, few comparative studies examine different control-sharing approaches in assistive robotics. This research presents a control design for a robotic smart wheelchair enabling flexible implementation and evaluation of multiple control-sharing methods. The authors implemented four control-sharing paradigms and conducted experiments comparing them against teleoperation using different control interfaces across multiple sessions. Key findings indicate that task performance varies by interface, performance improves with greater autonomy (though differences diminish at higher autonomy levels), and user effort decreases with increased autonomy assistance. The utilization of autonomy differs substantially across paradigms but not interfaces. Session 2 shows consistent performance improvements over Session 1. Subjective feedback reveals both convergences and divergences between individuals with spinal cord injury and uninjured participants. No single paradigm emerges as superior, suggesting multiple control options should accommodate individual user requirements.
relevance_note: Systematic comparison of four shared-control paradigms with SCI participants, directly addressing variable autonomy levels and their effect on effort and performance.

title: Autonomy in Rehabilitation Robotics: An Intersection
venue: Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems
abstract: The paper examines how robotic systems with autonomous capabilities can be integrated into rehabilitation devices to help individuals with motor impairments. While rehabilitation robots exist for both therapeutic purposes and functional task replacement, they rarely incorporate autonomous decision-making. The author argues that robotics autonomy able to perceive the external world and reason about high-level control decisions could reduce operational demands on users, particularly those with severe impairments. The work surveys control challenges in prosthetics, wheelchairs, and robotic arms, then reviews research introducing autonomy to these systems. Key topics include shared-control paradigms, intent inference, and customized assistance. The paper highlights critical clinical considerations often overlooked by the autonomy community and proposes integrating rehabilitation with functional assistance as a future goal.
relevance_note: Comprehensive survey of autonomy in assistive devices including wheelchairs, framing shared control, intent inference, and variable autonomy as core challenges.

title: Turning Assistive Machines into Assistive Robots
venue: Proc. SPIE 9370, Quantum Sensing and Nanophotonic Devices XII
abstract: The paper addresses a fundamental paradox: individuals with severe motor impairments often struggle most to operate assistive devices that could enhance their quality of life. Argall proposes incorporating robotic autonomy into assistive machines to offload some of the control burden from the user. The work examines how robots can leverage synthetic sensing, reasoning, and action capabilities to bridge gaps created by sensory, motor, or cognitive impairments. The paper surveys ongoing projects exploring shared control paradigms, user intent estimation, autonomous goal perception, and machine learning applications within assistive robotics—with emphasis on enabling users to maintain meaningful control while benefiting from automation.
relevance_note: Seminal position paper articulating the shared-autonomy research agenda for assistive devices, with wheelchair as the primary example platform.

title: Shared autonomy via hindsight optimization for teleoperation and teaming
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
abstract: In shared autonomy, a user and autonomous system work together to achieve shared goals. To collaborate effectively, the autonomous system must know the user's goal. Most prior works follow a predict-then-act model, first predicting the user's goal with high confidence, then assisting given that goal. Unfortunately, confidently predicting the user's goal may not be possible until they have nearly achieved it, causing predict-then-act methods to provide little assistance. The work formalizes shared autonomy as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), providing assistance that minimizes the expected cost-to-go with an unknown goal. As solving this POMDP optimally is intractable, the authors use hindsight optimization to approximate. Applied to both shared-control teleoperation and human-robot teaming, compared with predict-then-act methods, the method achieves goals faster, requires less user input, decreases user idling time, and results in fewer user-robot collisions.
relevance_note: Foundational POMDP-based shared autonomy framework using hindsight optimization, directly applicable to wheelchair goal-directed navigation under intent uncertainty.

title: Shared Autonomy via Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: In shared autonomy, user input is combined with semi-autonomous control to achieve a common goal. The goal is often unknown ex-ante, so prior work enables agents to infer the goal from user input and assist with the task. Such methods tend to assume some combination of knowledge of the dynamics of the environment, the user's policy given their goal, and the set of possible goals the user might target, which limits their application to real-world scenarios. We propose a deep reinforcement learning framework for model-free shared autonomy that lifts these assumptions. We use human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning with neural network function approximation to learn an end-to-end mapping from environmental observation and user input to agent action values, with task reward as the only form of supervision. Controlled studies with 12 users playing a video game and a pilot study with 4 users flying a real quadrotor demonstrate the ability of the algorithm to assist users with real-time control tasks in which the agent implicitly infers user intent from input. The assisted user completes the task more effectively than the user or an autonomous agent could on their own.
relevance_note: Proposes a model-free deep RL approach to shared autonomy that makes no assumptions about user goals or dynamics, directly relevant to wheelchair shared control without pre-defined intent models.

title: User-adapted plan recognition and user-adapted shared control: A Bayesian approach to semi-autonomous wheelchair driving
abstract: Many elderly and physically impaired people experience difficulties when maneuvering a powered wheelchair. To ease maneuvering, powered wheelchairs have been equipped with sensors, additional computing power and intelligence by various research groups. This paper presents a Bayesian approach to maneuvering assistance for wheelchair driving that can be adapted to a specific user. More specifically, the proposed framework is able to model and estimate even complex user intents (wheelchair maneuvers that the driver has in mind), explicitly takes uncertainty on the user's intent into account, and incorporates user-specific properties and uncertainty on the user's intent when taking assistive actions, such that assistance is tailored to the user's driving skills. Additionally, this decision making is modeled as a greedy Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Experimental results with healthy subjects and Cerebral Palsy subjects show that the system can improve navigation outcome for people with disability and leads to around 10% faster completion of tasks compared to local obstacle avoidance systems.
relevance_note: Foundational Bayesian/POMDP framework for user-adapted intent recognition and shared control in wheelchairs, with experiments on users with Cerebral Palsy.

title: POMDP-based long-term user intention prediction for wheelchair navigation
venue: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
abstract: This paper presents an intelligent decision-making agent to assist wheelchair users in their daily navigation activities. Recent research has seen a move towards more intelligent systems that focus on forecasting users' intentions based on current and past actions. The key contribution of this work is the ability to predict the users' intended destination at a larger scale, that of a typical office arena. The system relies on minimal user input—obtained from a standard wheelchair joystick—in conjunction with a learned Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), to estimate and subsequently drive the user to their destination.
relevance_note: Early POMDP model for predicting wheelchair user destination at building scale using minimal joystick input, a landmark in intent prediction for powered wheelchairs.

title: Collaborative control for a robotic wheelchair: evaluation of performance, attention, and workload
venue: IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part B (Cybernetics)
abstract: The research addresses wheelchair users struggling with safe operation by proposing a collaborative control system. This mechanism uses prediction algorithms to identify driver intentions and adjusts control inputs when necessary. The evaluation combined performance metrics with eye-tracking and secondary task analysis. Results demonstrated that users without assistance experienced collisions, whereas those with the collaborative controller achieved safer driving while maintaining reduced cognitive workload. The authors emphasize potential applications in shared control systems, particularly for brain-machine interfaces where low-frequency user input is involved.
relevance_note: Evaluates collaborative wheelchair control using eye-tracking and secondary task analysis to measure cognitive workload reduction—a key metric for shared autonomy systems.

title: Human-wheelchair collaboration through prediction of intention and adaptive assistance
venue: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
abstract: Powered wheelchair users want to be active drivers rather than passengers, and while in some situations (varying from person to person) they may require assistance, research is being conducted into the development of smart wheelchairs. This paper examines how collaborative control techniques can offer users help as needed. The collaboration is built by predicting user intentions and responding to these predictions with adaptable levels of assistance. The design approach is based around each individual user's abilities and desires, maximizing the amount of control given to the user.
relevance_note: Early formulation of adaptive assistance for wheelchairs via intent prediction, establishing user-centered principles that guided subsequent shared autonomy research.

title: Wheelchair collaborative control for disabled users navigating indoors
abstract: This research proposes a shared control method for robotic wheelchairs enabling simultaneous contributions from both users and assistive systems. Rather than switching control between person and robot, the approach weights their commands according to their respective local efficiencies and merges them through reactive navigation. Testing involved 18 volunteers with varying physical and cognitive disabilities in a home setting. Results indicated successful task completion and positive user/caregiver feedback, with statistical analysis (p=0.016) demonstrating meaningful performance improvements using this collaborative methodology.
relevance_note: Proposes an efficiency-weighting blending approach for continuous shared control tested with disabled users in a home environment.

title: Semi-autonomous mobility assistance for power wheelchair users navigating crowded environments
venue: IEEE International Conference on Rehabilitation Robotics (ICORR)
abstract: The research addresses challenges wheelchair users with cognitive or physical impairments encounter when maneuvering through crowded spaces. The team developed a collision-avoidance system using ultrasonic sensors that detects nearby obstacles and integrates user joystick input to generate optimal motion vectors. According to the abstract, this approach reduces the cognitive load on the user and enables them to navigate complex environments through simplified control inputs, helping prevent accidental collisions caused by imprecise joystick control or delayed reaction times.
relevance_note: Addresses cognitive load reduction via semi-autonomous obstacle avoidance in crowded environments for powered wheelchair users.

title: Evaluation of an intelligent wheelchair system for older adults with cognitive impairments
abstract: The research describes development and testing of an add-on intelligent system designed to enhance powered wheelchair safety for cognitively impaired seniors. The system incorporates two primary features: vision-based collision prevention and audio-guided navigation assistance. A two-phase evaluation included environmental performance testing against typical long-term care facility obstacles, followed by user trials with older adults experiencing cognitive decline. Results demonstrated the system successfully detected obstacles in controlled settings and reduced collision frequency during user testing, while also lowering perceived workload. However, task completion time showed minimal improvement, and audio prompt adherence remained suboptimal in some participants, indicating opportunities for continued refinement in usability aspects of the technology.
relevance_note: Clinical evaluation of intelligent wheelchair assistance specifically for cognitively impaired older adults, measuring collision frequency and perceived workload.

title: Design and validation of an intelligent wheelchair towards a clinically-functional outcome
abstract: The research addresses mobility challenges for wheelchair users by developing an intelligent powered wheelchair platform. The team created three major contributions: software architecture for navigation in confined spaces, a decision-theoretic speech-control system, and the Robotic Wheelchair Skills Test evaluation protocol. Testing involved 17 subjects across 32 sessions totaling 25 hours and 9 kilometers of operation. Results demonstrated the navigation system reduced collisions by more than 60% compared to other recent intelligent wheelchair platforms. Performance with autonomous mode showed minimal decline—4% decrease in performance and 3% in safety metrics—when compared to conventional joystick control, despite minimal training with the intelligent system compared to years of joystick experience.
relevance_note: SmartWheeler clinical validation study using a bespoke Robotic Wheelchair Skills Test, establishing evaluation standards for shared-control wheelchair systems.

title: Intelligent wheelchair control strategies for older adults with cognitive impairment: user attitudes, needs, and preferences
abstract: Intelligent powered wheelchairs can increase mobility and independence for older adults with cognitive impairment by providing collision avoidance and navigation support. The level and type of control desired by this target population during intelligent wheelchair use had not been previously explored. A study was conducted with a mock intelligent wheelchair offering three different modes of user control. Users wanted to be in the loop during wheelchair operation and/or high-level decision making, and also provided specific contexts where an autonomous wheelchair would be helpful. Participants identified benefits of and concerns with intelligent wheelchairs, along with desired features and functionality.
relevance_note: User study revealing preferences for shared (not full) autonomy among older adults with cognitive impairment, directly informing adjustable autonomy level design.

title: Learning assistance by demonstration: smart mobility with shared control and paired haptic controllers
abstract: This research presents a framework, probabilistic model, and algorithm for learning shared control policies by observing an assistant, referred to as Learning Assistance by Demonstration (LAD). The approach develops an efficient online mixture of experts (OME) algorithm, based on sparse Gaussian processes, for learning the assistive policy. The LAD methodology is coupled with a novel paired-haptic-controllers setup for helping smart wheelchair users navigate their environment. The system learns how and when to help based on demonstrations, capturing the nuanced decision-making of a skilled human assistant.
relevance_note: Introduces Learning Assistance by Demonstration for wheelchair shared control, enabling personalized assistance policies learned from a single human demonstration via Gaussian processes.

title: Learning Shared Control by Demonstration for Personalized Wheelchair Assistance
abstract: This paper presents a method to learn shared control policies from demonstrations offered by a human assistant. A Gaussian process regression model is trained to continuously regulate the level of assistance between the user and the system, given the user's previous and current actions and the state of the environment. The assistance policy is learned after only a single human demonstration (one-shot). The robotic assistance was not perceived very differently from actual human assistance, and haptic cues from partners did not cause subjects to feel an increased level of work load, nor did they affect subjects' comfort or enjoyment level.
relevance_note: One-shot learning of personalized wheelchair assistance policies via haptic demonstration, evaluated with human participants measuring workload and comfort.

title: Model-based shared control approach for a power wheelchair driving assistance system using a force feedback joystick
abstract: This research presents a haptic-assisted system for power wheelchair users employing a model-based shared control methodology. The system combines robust control with supervisory functions to distribute control responsibilities between the user and the assistance system. The framework includes two operational modes: Normal Driving Assistance reduces user effort through haptic feedback, while Obstacle Avoidance Assistance engages when collision risks emerge. The system employs Unknown Input Observers for Takagi-Sugeno fuzzy models to interpret user intentions via hand torques and joystick position. A conflict management algorithm enables users to override system recommendations, preserving their agency as primary decision-makers. Testing via human-hardware simulation validated the system's effectiveness in balancing safety, comfort, and user autonomy.
relevance_note: Model-based shared control with haptic force feedback joystick providing continuous adjustable assistance while preserving user override authority in power wheelchair navigation.

title: Shared Control of an Electric Wheelchair Considering Physical Functions and Driving Motivation
venue: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
abstract: Individuals with severe physical impairments face challenges operating electric wheelchairs, particularly requiring fine steering abilities. While automatic driving offers a partial solution, over-reliance on it undermines maintenance of residual physical functions. This research developed a shared control system that dynamically balances user and machine control authority, utilizing the operating capabilities of users while preserving their motivation to actively participate. The investigators analyzed operating characteristics of individuals with severe impairments and proposed a reinforcement learning-based method to adjust control weights between user and system. Experimental outcomes demonstrated that the system gradually calibrated control distribution, enabling safe wheelchair operation while fully employing user input signals. The findings revealed that shared control effectiveness varied significantly based on user type and characteristics.
relevance_note: Addresses the under-studied issue of preserving user residual capabilities and intrinsic motivation within shared control through RL-based dynamic control weight adjustment.

title: Assisted navigation for a brain-actuated intelligent wheelchair
abstract: The researchers present an Assistive Navigation System for a robotic wheelchair controlled through a brain-computer interface. Their approach uses a two-layer collaborative control mechanism that manages both user commands and automated navigation decisions. The system enables user input at critical points—intersections, obstacle-related course changes, and deadlocks—while matching user intent to appropriate steering commands based on operator competence and environmental awareness. Testing with P300-based BCI technology involved ten able-bodied participants plus one individual with cerebral palsy across structured and dynamic environments. Results demonstrated that all participants were able to successfully operate the device, validating the robustness of both the BCI and navigation systems.
relevance_note: Demonstrates two-layer shared control for a BCI-actuated wheelchair, dynamically arbitrating between user P300 commands and autonomous navigation based on context.

title: Towards BCI-actuated smart wheelchair system
abstract: This research presents an intelligent wheelchair system controlled through brain signals that enables severely motor-disabled individuals to navigate and complete tasks. The system combines an omnidirectional wheelchair, a robotic arm, and real-time object recognition using the YOLO algorithm. Users confirm targets detected in their environment via P300-based brain-computer interface signals. An expert system plans appropriate actions for identified objects—for example, opening doors before passage or retrieving items. Testing involved three patients (cerebral infarction, spinal injury, stroke) and four healthy participants who successfully completed daily living simulations including approaching a person for conversation, navigating through doorways, and retrieving beverages. Results demonstrated the system achieved 100% task completion with minimal errors, validating its practical utility for rehabilitation applications.
relevance_note: BCI-actuated wheelchair with shared autonomy integrating P300 intent signals, autonomous object recognition, and expert-system action planning for complex daily tasks.

title: Wheelchair navigation assisted by Human-Machine shared-control and a P300-based Brain Computer Interface
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
abstract: This paper presents a new shared-control approach for assistive mobile robots, using Brain Computer Interface (BCI) as the Human-Machine Interface (HMI). It proposes a P300-based paradigm that allows the selection of brain-actuated commands to steer a robotic wheelchair. To alleviate user effort, low-level commands are only issued when there are dynamic changes of the environment or when ambiguous situations occur. A two-layer shared-control approach is proposed to obtain a safe and effective navigation of the wheelchair, receiving user commands that are issued sparsely.
relevance_note: Introduces sparse BCI command issuance combined with autonomous navigation through a two-layer shared control architecture, reducing cognitive and physical user effort.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Smart Wheelchairs: Past, Present and Future
abstract: A smart wheelchair (SW) is a power wheelchair to which computers, sensors, and assistive technology are attached. This paper systematically presents the international SW research effort, starting with an introduction to powered wheelchairs and the communities they serve, and discusses in detail the SW and associated technological innovations with an emphasis on the most researched areas, generating the most interest for future research and development. The review spans a decade of innovation in smart wheelchair technology and identifies promising directions for future development, with a focus on improving mobility for individuals with disabilities.
relevance_note: Comprehensive decade-spanning review of smart wheelchair technology providing essential context for shared autonomy research landscape and research gaps.

title: Mini-review: Robotic wheelchair taxonomy and readiness
abstract: The paper introduces a framework for categorizing robotic wheelchair devices and evaluating their development stage. The authors conducted a comprehensive review spanning 2,797 articles across seven databases, identifying 205 relevant articles and 4 review papers. Their taxonomy combines powered wheelchair standards with mobile robot specifications, the ICF model, and the PHAATE framework. The analysis reveals that innovations in this field have been slow to translate into the marketplace, with most prototypes remaining at proof-of-concept phases rather than advancing to real-world deployment or commercial availability.
relevance_note: Provides a standardized taxonomy for robotic wheelchairs and highlights the gap between research prototypes and market-ready shared-autonomy devices.

title: CoNav Chair: Design of a ROS-based Smart Wheelchair for Shared Control Navigation in the Built Environment
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd ISARC (International Symposium on Automation and Robotics in Construction)
abstract: The researchers developed an intelligent wheelchair system utilizing the Robot Operating System framework that combines shared control navigation with obstacle avoidance capabilities. The system aims to help people with disabilities achieve greater independence while maintaining user trust and efficiency. Their approach balances between full autonomous operation and manual control, addressing limitations in existing powered wheelchair designs. Testing in typical indoor environments demonstrated that the integrated hardware-software solution effectively promotes both user autonomy and confidence in assistive mobility technologies for real-world settings.
relevance_note: Recent ROS-based shared control wheelchair prototype with obstacle avoidance, providing a modern implementation baseline for indoor built-environment navigation.

title: CoNav Chair: Development and Evaluation of a Shared Control based Wheelchair for the Built Environment
abstract: The paper presents a robotic wheelchair system addressing mobility needs for people with disabilities. The CoNav Chair implements a shared control navigation and obstacle avoidance framework built on the Robot Operating System (ROS). Rather than choosing between purely manual or fully autonomous operation, the system offers a hybrid approach. A usability study with 21 unimpaired participants tested three navigation modes in an indoor building environment. The shared control mode demonstrated superior performance, achieving significantly fewer collisions while matching autonomous and manual modes on completion time, trajectory efficiency, and smoothness. Users rated the shared control approach as safer and more efficient based on subjective assessments.
relevance_note: Controlled evaluation of three navigation modes (manual, shared, autonomous) in an indoor environment with 21 participants, using both objective and subjective usability metrics.

title: Prediction of user preference over shared-control paradigms for a robotic wheelchair
venue: IEEE International Conference on Rehabilitation Robotics (ICORR)
abstract: The research addresses how to incorporate user preferences into powered wheelchair design. Rather than continuously asking users for feedback during operation, the authors developed a machine learning model to predict preferred control methods based on objective performance metrics. Their approach correlates task execution data—including effort, safety, performance, and utilization—with subjective user evaluations across different autonomous wheelchair control paradigms. The study involved both spinal cord injured and uninjured participants, demonstrating that the model enables continuous preference tracking and potentially customized autonomy adjusted to individual users' needs.
relevance_note: Applies machine learning to predict which shared-control paradigm a user prefers from objective performance signals, enabling implicit personalization of autonomy levels.

title: Federated Learning from Demonstration for Active Assistance to Smart Wheelchair Users
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
abstract: Learning from Demonstration (LfD) is an approach to empower robots with autonomy where a robot learns a policy to solve tasks from demonstrations provided by a human teacher without explicit programming. A key use case is endowing smart robotic wheelchairs with active assistance to navigation, allowing them to learn to infer short-term destinations anywhere without needing to build a map of the environment beforehand. To address the difficulty of generalizing robot behaviors to environments other than those used for training, the researchers proposed learning from crowds involving diverse teachers in real environments through Federated Learning from Demonstration (FLfD). The federated models showed good generalization ability, performing well when evaluated on a domain that was not used for training.
relevance_note: Introduces federated learning from demonstration for wheelchair navigation assistance, enabling collaborative policy learning across diverse real-world environments without centralized data.

title: Intentional User Adaptation to Shared Control Assistance
venue: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI)
abstract: This paper challenges the typical assumption in shared control approaches that user behavior remains constant despite assistance. Instead, it shows that users both change their control behavior when assistance is added and describe these changes as responses to the new system dynamics. In a computer-based bubble popping study, participants reported changing their strategies with different levels of assistance, and analysis of their actual control input validated this change. Additionally, the researchers conducted a public-space user study in which participants controlled a robot to pick up a cup despite the presence of assistance that directed them towards incorrect goals, yet participants still succeeded on the task despite the changes in dynamics introduced by the assistance. These results motivate further research in user-centered design and evaluation of assistive systems that treat the user as intentional.
relevance_note: Challenges the static-user assumption in shared control, showing users actively adapt strategies in response to assistance—critical for evaluating wheelchair shared autonomy systems.

title: Adaptable navigational assistance for intelligent wheelchairs by means of an implicit personalized user model
abstract: Elderly and disabled people can experience considerable difficulties when driving a powered wheelchair. Several intelligent wheelchairs have been developed to provide navigational assistance, with control shared between the user and the intelligent assistance. However, the problem with existing intelligent wheelchairs is that the rules for assistance are hard-coded and not adaptable to the personal handicap and needs of a specific user. The research proposes a new, more user-centered approach to shared wheelchair control using a neural network to model a personalized shared-assistance system, featuring standard smart driving modes such as zero assistance and obstacle avoidance, which automatically modifies the path selected by the user to drive around detected obstacles.
relevance_note: Introduces implicit personalized user modeling via neural networks to adapt shared control assistance level to individual wheelchair users' handicap and needs.

title: Shared autonomy for cognitive load regulation in autonomous wheelchairs
abstract: This study advances human-machine partnership design in assistive mobility by introducing a cognitive digital twin framework for autonomous wheelchair systems that investigates dynamic collaboration mechanisms between users with motor impairments and autonomous driving systems, focusing on situational awareness regulation and adaptive autonomy allocation. Through Unity-based digital-twin simulation experiments with 52 participants, the research evaluated multi-level human-machine interface designs, finding that progressive information presentation significantly reduced reaction times by 23.5% and improved task accuracy for up to 98.1%. Shared and supervisory control strategies with higher automation levels markedly enhanced user experience and operational efficiency while lowering cognitive load.
relevance_note: Uses cognitive digital twin simulation with 52 participants to quantify how shared vs. supervisory autonomy levels affect cognitive load, reaction time, and task accuracy in wheelchair navigation.
